meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas. doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.title: Is autophagy actually REQUIRED for the mammalian lifespan benefit?
data.gap: Autophagy is assumed to mediate longevity but shown directly only in fly and worm - BJE2010 (rapamycin extends fly lifespan through autophagy and reduced translation) and HAN2008 (blocking autophagy genes abolishes the lifespan extension produced by dietary restriction in C. elegans) - plus Atg5 overexpression in mouse (PYO2013), which shows sufficiency, not necessity. No study IN THIS CORPUS tests whether BLOCKING autophagy abolishes rapamycin's mammalian lifespan extension - the epistasis experiment that would settle it has not been done in a mammal as far as this Atlas holds. Note the shape of the gap: it is specifically MAMMALIAN. The causal experiment does exist in invertebrates, which is why this card cites two of them. Gaps in this Atlas are computed against this corpus, not against PubMed. Note that this particular claim also survives an external check - a targeted PubMed query for an autophagy-deficient x rapamycin x mammalian lifespan experiment returns no records - but the wording should still say what it can support.
data.gap_beginner: Autophagy (the cell's self-cleanup process) is widely assumed to be why blocking mTOR extends lifespan, but that's only been directly shown in flies and worms, plus one mouse study that boosted autophagy a different way. No study in this Atlas tests what happens to rapamycin's lifespan benefit in mice that can't do autophagy at all.
data.changed_since_written: Nothing has answered the question, but the experiment as proposed turns out not to be runnable. Inducible whole-body Atg7 deletion in an adult mouse limits survival to two or three months through neurodegeneration and infection, plus fatal fasting hypoglycaemia (Karsli-Uzunbas, Cancer Discov 2014, PMID 24875857); a lifespan study needs about three years. A null result would be unreadable — no benefit, or an animal that died of something rapamycin cannot fix — and chronic rapamycin also inhibits mTORC2, so failure in an Atg7 knockout would not implicate autophagy cleanly either. In flies, rapamycin already acts through autophagy and translation in parallel (Bjedov, Cell Metab 2010, PMID 20074526), so the expected mammalian answer is partly, which a survival curve cannot resolve. A 2026 result bears on the mechanism without touching necessity: in human T cells under genotoxic stress, rapamycin and other mTOR inhibitors suppressed senescence and improved survival by lowering DNA lesion burden, and explicitly not by slowing protein synthesis, halting division or stimulating autophagy (Kell, Aging Cell 2026, PMID 41524558). One cell type and one stressor, with no lifespan readout — but it is a direct demonstration that a geroprotective effect of rapamycin can run entirely around autophagy.
data.still_open: Necessity, still untested in any mammal. The mammalian evidence runs one way only: raising autophagy extends life (Becn1-F121A knock-in, Fernandez, Nature 2018, PMID 29849149; Atg5 overexpression, +17.2% median, Pyo, Nat Commun 2013, PMID 23939249). Sufficiency is shown; necessity is not.
data.hypothesis: Autophagy is necessary: rapamycin will FAIL to extend lifespan in autophagy-deficient (e.g. inducible Atg7-KO) mice.
data.hypothesis_beginner: Educated guess: autophagy is actually required – mice that can't perform autophagy should get no lifespan benefit from rapamycin, even though the drug still works everywhere else.
data.how_to_test: Occlusion rather than ablation. Does rapamycin still extend lifespan in Becn1-F121A mice, which carry ENHANCED basal autophagy and are healthy? Note the wording: the cited work reports enhanced basal autophagy, not a demonstrated saturation ceiling, so the experiment cannot be read as adding rapamycin on top of a maximum. Define the three questions separately before running it, because they are different estimands and one design does not answer all three: NECESSITY (does blocking autophagy abolish the benefit), SUFFICIENCY (does raising autophagy alone reproduce it) and MEDIATED FRACTION (what share of the benefit runs through autophagy, which needs a mediation model, not a survival comparison). Read the result with care: additivity is only suggestive, not decisive. If rapamycin adds nothing on top of enhanced autophagy, that is consistent with autophagy carrying much of the benefit; but two interventions can be additive or non-additive for reasons unrelated to a shared mechanism (Gkioni, Nature Aging 2025, PMID 40437307), so the experiment narrows the question rather than settling the share. Use validated autophagic-flux measures rather than inferring flux from a genotype. Supporting designs: tissue-restricted Atg7 deletion, which survives into old age (Yuan, Aging Cell 2020, PMID 32212304), and autophagy-hypomorphic rather than null backgrounds. One caveat on the Becn1 line: its longevity phenotype is abolished by a chronic high-phosphate diet (Shi, FASEB J 2020, PMID 31908069), so diet must be controlled.
revision_log: 2026-09-04: The basis previously read 'No study tests whether...', an absence claim about the whole literature; now scoped to this corpus.

2026-09-21: MEL2003 was cited as the worm evidence. It tested bec-1 in daf-2 mutants (the insulin/IGF-1 pathway, not TOR and not dietary restriction), so it did not support the claim; HAN2008 replaced it.

2026-10-03: EIS2016 added - mouse evidence that cardiomyocyte Atg5 is required for spermidine-induced cardioprotection and lifespan extension, addressing the necessity-of-autophagy question for a geroprotector other than rapamycin.

2026-10-03: EIS2009 added - invertebrate necessity evidence that autophagy is required for a lifespan-extending intervention, leaving the mammalian necessity question and the rapamycin-specific case untouched (yeast, fly, worm and human immune cells; no mammalian lifespan data).

2026-10-07: KEL2026 (Kell 2026, PMID 41524558) added to What_Changed - in human T cells rapamycin's anti-senescence effect was shown to bypass autophagy. Mechanism in cells only; the necessity-for-lifespan question is unchanged. Added because the card otherwise leaves the impression that no evidence separates a geroprotective rapamycin effect from autophagy (revision of all 17 cards against the literature).

2026-10-10: Audit A07 (remaining work). The proposed test described Becn1-F121A mice as carrying 'maximal basal autophagy'. Fernandez 2018 reports ENHANCED basal autophagy; enhanced is not an experimentally established maximum, and the saturation assumption was doing real work in how the result would be read. Corrected, and necessity, sufficiency and mediated fraction are now named as three separate estimands to be defined in advance, with validated flux measures rather than flux inferred from a genotype.
